The Short-tailed shearwater Ardenna tenuirostris exhibits a fascinating suite of life-history traits shaped by its extreme migratory lifestyle and colonial breeding habits in the Southern Hemisphere. Eggs are typically incubated at a constant internal temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], a thermal regime that produces a hatchling after approximately 53 days [ab = approximately 53 days]. This prolonged incubation period, one of the longest among procellariiform birds, reflects the large yolk-rich egg that must sustain the developing embryo. Upon hatching, the neonate emerges with a wet weight at birth of 77 grams [Wwb = 77 grams], a relatively modest mass that represents a small fraction of the ultimate adult size. The chick is entirely dependent on both parents for warmth and food during its initial weeks, receiving regular meals of lipid-rich stomach oil and partially digested fish and squid.

The nestling phase is characterized by a spectacular period of somatic growth under the intense metabolic conditions maintained by parental provisioning. During this stage, at a core body temperature of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C], the chick accumulates tissue at a remarkable rate, ultimately reaching an asymptotic wet weight prior to fledging of approximately 700 grams [Wwi = approximately 700 grams]. This ultimate wet weight is considerably greater than the mean adult mass of 499.4 grams reported for the species, indicating that fledglings often depart the burrow carrying significant fat reserves that buffer them against the energetic challenges of their first foraging flights. The developmental trajectory from a 77 gram [Wwb = 77 gram] hatchling to a 700 gram [Wwi = 700 gram] chick represents a nearly tenfold increase in body mass achieved over a relatively short interval, a growth efficiency that underscores the productivity of the marine foraging grounds utilized by the adults.

Fledging in A. tenuirostris occurs once the chick has completed its feather development and achieved sufficient flight muscle mass, a milestone that arrives 82 days after hatching [tx = 82 days after hatching] under the typical thermal conditions of the burrow, maintained at approximately 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C]. This period of 82 days post-hatch is critical, as it marks the transition from a sedentary, parent-fed existence to a fully independent pelagic lifestyle. Upon departure, the fledgling is essentially on its own, with no further parental guidance or provisioning. The timing of this event is tightly synchronized with the austral summer, ensuring that oceanic prey resources are at their seasonal peak. The young birds then embark on a long-distance migration to the North Pacific, a journey that requires the substantial energy stores accumulated during the nestling period. This life stage represents a major physiological bottleneck with high mortality rates.

The journey to sexual maturity is a protracted process for this species, with individuals not attaining full reproductive status until several years after hatching. Puberty, defined here as the onset of gonadal maturation and the development of breeding plumage, is reached at 246 days since birth [tp = 246 days since birth] when the birds are experiencing a typical active metabolic body temperature of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C]. However, reaching physiological puberty does not equate to immediate breeding success. The time since birth at first brood is considerably longer, estimated at 5 years since birth [tR = 5 years since birth] under similar thermal conditions of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C]. This delay between the attainment of puberty and actual first reproduction is common among long-lived seabirds and is thought to reflect the time required to perfect foraging skills, establish a burrow site, and secure a mate within dense breeding colonies.

The overall pace of life in the Short-tailed shearwater is best encapsulated by its maximum recorded lifespan and its annual reproductive output. Under the warm metabolic conditions of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C], the oldest documented individuals in the wild have been recorded at approximately 39.9 years [am = approximately 39.9 years] of age, a remarkable longevity for a bird of its size that places it among the most enduring of the Procellariidae. This extended lifespan is coupled with a comparatively low annual reproductive rate; females typically produce a single egg per clutch [N_R_i = single egg per clutch] and one clutch per year [F_R_i = one clutch per year], which represents the maximum reproductive rate for the species given its chick-rearing constraints. This strategy of high adult survival and low fecundity is characteristic of K-selected species that inhabit unpredictable marine environments where the cost of reproduction is high and the failure rate of individual breeding attempts is significant.
